q-36306.name: Question 1
q-36306.problem:
Given the function  $g(x,y)=({x}^{2}+y)^{2}$, find its directional derivative at the
point $A(-1,1)$ in the direction that's towards the point $B(3,4).$
q-36306.worked_solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨3,4⟩-⟨-1,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4,3⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}}}⟨4,3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨4,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+y)^{2},\,\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+y)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨4x({x}^{2}+y),\,2({x}^{2}+y)⟩ \\ ∇g(-1,1) & =⟨4\cdot (-1)\cdot ((-1)^{2}+1),2\cdot ((-1)^{2}+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-8,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(-1,1) & =∇g(-1,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨-8,4⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{4}{5},\frac{3}{5}⟩ \\  & =-8\cdot \frac{4}{5}+4\cdot \frac{3}{5} \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

q-86533.name: Question 2
q-86533.problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=(2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})^{2}$ at the point $A(-1,-1)$ in the direction towards the point $B(2,0).$
q-86533.worked_solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨2,0⟩-⟨-1,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨3,1⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}}}⟨3,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟨3,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})^{2},\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨8x(2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}),\,36{y}^{3}-24{x}^{2}y⟩ \\ ∇f(-1,-1) & =⟨8(-1)\cdot (2(-1)^{2}-3(-1)^{2}),36(-1)^{3}-24(-1)^{2}(-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨8,-12⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(-1,-1) & =∇f(-1,-1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨8,-12⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟩ \\  & =8\cdot \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}-12\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{10}} \\  & =\frac{6\sqrt{10}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-86430.name: Question 3
q-86430.problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=(2{x}^{2}-y)^{2}$ at the point $A(-1,1)$ in the direction towards the point $B(-2,2).$
q-86430.worked_solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨-2,2⟩-⟨-1,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,1⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}}⟨-1,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-y)^{2},\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-y)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨16{x}^{3}-8xy,\,2y-4{x}^{2}⟩ \\ ∇f(-1,1) & =⟨16(-1)^{3}-8(-1)(1),\,2(1)-4(-1)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-8,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(-1,1) & =∇f(-1,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨-8,-2⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟩ \\  & =(-8)\cdot (-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})-2\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}) \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The directional derivative fu′(a,b) of a function f(x,y) at the point (a,b) in the direction of the vector v is given by

fu′(a,b)=∇f(a,b)⋅u

where u is a unit vector in the direction of v.

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

AB→=⟨−2,2⟩−⟨−1,1⟩=⟨−1,1⟩u=AB→‖AB→‖=1(−1)2+12⟨−1,1⟩=12⟨−1,1⟩

∇f(x,y)=⟨∂∂x(2x2−y)2,∂∂y(2x2−y)2⟩=⟨16x3−8xy,2y−4x2⟩∇f(−1,1)=⟨16(−1)3−8(−1)(1),2(1)−4(−1)2⟩=⟨−8,−2⟩

q-83552.name: Question 4
q-83552.problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=2i+j.$
q-83552.worked_solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{5} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(2i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }j \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡y+\frac{y}{x})\,i+(\frac{x}{y}+\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\,j \\ ∇\,f(1,1) & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡1+\frac{1}{1})\,i+(\frac{1}{1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\,j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,1) & =∇\,f(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =(i+j)\cdot (\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}j) \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 2+1\cdot 1}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-130258.name: Question 5
q-130258.problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-6xy+{y}^{2}$ at the point $(-1,3)$ in the direction of the vector $v=i+j.$
q-130258.worked_solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{2} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(-1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-6xy+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-6xy+{y}^{2})\text{ }j \\  & =(2x-6y)\,i+(2y-6x)j \\ ∇\,f(-1,3) & =(2(-1)-6(3))\,i+(2(3)-6(-1))j \\  & =-20\,i+12\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(-1,3) & =∇\,f(-1,3)\cdot u \\  & =(-20\,i+12\,j)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i+j) \\  & =\frac{-20(1)+12(1)}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =-\frac{8}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =-4\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-83562.name: Question 6
q-83562.problem: In what direction does the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+{x}^{2}y$ decrease most rapidly at the point $(\pi ,0)?$
q-83562.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ decreases most rapidly in the direction opposite to that of its gradient.

So, we compute $-∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(\pi ,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}-∇f(x,y) & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+{x}^{2}y)\text{ }i-\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+{x}^{2}y)\text{ }j \\  & =-(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+2xy)\text{ }i-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+{x}^{2})\text{ }j \\ -∇f(\pi ,0) & =-(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡0+2\cdot \pi \cdot 0)\text{ }i+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡0+{\pi }^{2})\text{ }j \\  & =i-{\pi }^{2}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

q-83562.html:
Question 6
?

In what direction does the function f(x,y)=sin⁡xcos⁡y+x2y decrease most rapidly at the point (π,0)?

a
 π2i+2πj
b
 πi+πj
c
 i−π2j
d
 π2i−j
e
 i−πj
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

At a given point, a function f(x,y) decreases most rapidly in the direction opposite to that of its gradient.

So, we compute −∇f(x,y) and evaluate it at the point (π,0):

−∇f(x,y)=−∂∂x(sin⁡xcos⁡y+x2y) i−∂∂y(sin⁡xcos⁡y+x2y) j=−(cos⁡xcos⁡y+2xy) i−(−sin⁡xsin⁡y+x2) j−∇f(π,0)=−(cos⁡πcos⁡0+2⋅π⋅0) i+(−sin⁡πsin⁡0+π2) j=i−π2j

Therefore, the function decreases most rapidly in the direction of i−π2j.

q-86540.name: Question 7
q-86540.problem: In what direction does the function $g(x,y,z)=4{z}^{2}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-y)$ increase most rapidly at the point $(2,-1,0)?$
q-86540.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $g(x,y,z)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇g(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at the point $(2,-1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{z}^{2}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-y)),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(4{z}^{2}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-y)),\,\frac{∂}{∂z}(4{z}^{2}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-y))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{x-y},\,-\frac{2}{x-y},\,8z⟩ \\ ∇g(2,-1,0) & =⟨\frac{2}{2-(-1)},\,-\frac{2}{2-(-1)},\,8\cdot 0⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{3},\,-\frac{2}{3},\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of $⟨\frac{2}{3},\,-\frac{2}{3},\,0⟩.$

Question 7
?

In what direction does the function g(x,y,z)=4z2+2ln⁡(x−y) increase most rapidly at the point (2,−1,0)?

a
⟨32,32,0⟩
b
−⟨23,23,0⟩
c
⟨23,−23,0⟩
d
⟨32,−23,2⟩
e
⟨23,−23,2⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

At a given point, a function g(x,y,z) increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute ∇g(x,y,z) and evaluate it at the point (2,−1,0):

∇g(x,y,z)=⟨∂∂x(4z2+2ln⁡(x−y)),∂∂y(4z2+2ln⁡(x−y)),∂∂z(4z2+2ln⁡(x−y))⟩=⟨2x−y,−2x−y,8z⟩∇g(2,−1,0)=⟨22−(−1),−22−(−1),8⋅0⟩=⟨23,−23,0⟩

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of ⟨23,−23,0⟩.

q-130279.name: Question 8
q-130279.problem: In what direction does the function $f(x,y)={e}^{2y}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2})$ increase most rapidly at the point $(\frac{\sqrt{\pi }}{2},0)?$
q-130279.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{2y}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2}))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2y}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2}))\,j \\  & =2x{e}^{2y}{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{2})\,i+2{e}^{2y}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2})\,j \\ ∇f(\frac{\sqrt{\pi }}{2},0) & =2(\frac{\sqrt{\pi }}{2}){e}^{0}{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,i+2{e}^{0}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,j \\  & =2\sqrt{\pi }\,i+2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of $2\sqrt{\pi }\,i+2\,j.$

q-83591.name: Question 9
q-83591.problem: In what direction does the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{tan}⁡y+2{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ decrease most rapidly at the point $(1,\frac{\pi }{4})?$
q-83591.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ decreases most rapidly in the direction opposite to that of its gradient.

So, we compute $-∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}-∇f(x,y) & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{tan}⁡y+2{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }i-\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{tan}⁡y+2{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }j \\  & =-(\operatorname{tan}⁡y+4x-\frac{1}{x})i-x{sec}^{2}⁡y\text{ }j \\ -∇f(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-(\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+4\cdot 1-\frac{1}{1})i-1\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\text{ }j \\  & =-4\,i-2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function decreases most rapidly in the direction of $-4\,i-2\,j.$

Question 9
?

In what direction does the function f(x,y)=xtan⁡y+2x2−ln⁡x decrease most rapidly at the point (1,π4)?

a
4i−12j
b
−4i−12j
c
−4i−2j
d
−6i−22j
e
−2i+14j
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

At a given point, a function f(x,y) decreases most rapidly in the direction opposite to that of its gradient.

So, we compute −∇f(x,y) and evaluate it at the point (1,π4):

−∇f(x,y)=−∂∂x(xtan⁡y+2x2−ln⁡x) i−∂∂y(xtan⁡y+2x2−ln⁡x) j=−(tan⁡y+4x−1x)i−xsec2⁡y j−∇f(1,π4)=−(tan⁡(π4)+4⋅1−11)i−1⋅sec2⁡(π4) j=−4i−2j

Therefore, the function decreases most rapidly in the direction of −4i−2j.

q-130270.name: Question 10
q-130270.problem: In what direction does the function $g(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xyz$ increase most rapidly at the point $(1,0,-2)?$
q-130270.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $g(x,y,z)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇g(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,0,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xyz),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xyz),\,\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xyz)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x-yz,\,2y-xz,\,2z-xy⟩ \\ ∇g(1,0,-2) & =⟨2(1)-0(-2),2(0)-1(-2),2(-2)-1(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,2,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of $⟨2,2,-4⟩.$

Question 10
?

In what direction does the function g(x,y,z)=x2+y2+z2−xyz increase most rapidly at the point (1,0,−2)?

a
⟨1,0,−2⟩
b
⟨1,−2,0⟩
c
⟨−1,−1,2⟩
d
⟨0,2,1⟩
e
⟨2,2,−4⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

At a given point, a function g(x,y,z) increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute ∇g(x,y,z) and evaluate it at the point (1,0,−2): ∇g(x,y,z)=⟨∂∂x(x2+y2+z2−xyz),∂∂y(x2+y2+z2−xyz),∂∂z(x2+y2+z2−xyz)⟩=⟨2x−yz,2y−xz,2z−xy⟩∇g(1,0,−2)=⟨2(1)−0(−2),2(0)−1(−2),2(−2)−1(0)⟩=⟨2,2,−4⟩

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of ⟨2,2,−4⟩.

q-37074.name: Question 11
q-37074.problem: Consider the function $g(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x).$ What is the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(e,\pi )$ in the direction in which the function increases most rapidly?
q-37074.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $g(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(e,\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x))⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\cdot \frac{y}{x},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{y\operatorname{cos}⁡(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{x},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)⟩ \\ ∇\,g(e,\pi ) & =⟨\frac{\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \operatorname{ln}⁡e)}{e},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡e\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \operatorname{ln}⁡e)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi }{e},\,1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\pi \cdot (-1)}{e},\,1\cdot (-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{\pi }{e},\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(e,\pi )$ in the direction of $∇g(e,\pi )$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖∇\,g(e,\pi )‖ & =‖⟨-\frac{\pi }{e},-1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{{e}^{2}}+1} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{\pi }^{2}+{e}^{2}}}{e}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11
?

Consider the function g(x,y)=sin⁡(yln⁡x). What is the rate of change of g(x,y) at the point (e,π) in the direction in which the function increases most rapidly?

a
π+ee
b
π2+e2π
c
π2+e2e
d
π4+e2π
e
π+ee
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

At a given point, a function g(x,y) increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute ∇g(x,y) and evaluate it at the point (e,π):

∇g(x,y)=⟨∂∂x(sin⁡(yln⁡x)),∂∂y(sin⁡(yln⁡x))⟩=⟨cos⁡(yln⁡x)⋅yx,cos⁡(yln⁡x)⋅ln⁡x⟩=⟨ycos⁡(yln⁡x)x,ln⁡xcos⁡(yln⁡x)⟩∇g(e,π)=⟨πcos⁡(πln⁡e)e,ln⁡ecos⁡(πln⁡e)⟩=⟨πcos⁡πe,1⋅cos⁡π⟩=⟨π⋅(−1)e,1⋅(−1)⟩=⟨−πe,−1⟩

Finally, the rate of change of g(x,y) at the point (e,π) in the direction of ∇g(e,π) is given by

‖∇g(e,π)‖=‖⟨−πe,−1⟩‖=π2e2+1=π2+e2e

q-130802.name: Question 12
q-130802.problem: Consider the function $g(x,y)={y}^{x}.$ What is the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(1,e)$ in the direction of the vector $v=⟨4,-3⟩?$
q-130802.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(1,e)$ in the direction of $v$ is equal to the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(1,e).$ 

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+(-3)^{2}}=5 \\ u & =\frac{1}{5}⟨4,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the gradient $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{x}),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{x})⟩ \\  & =⟨{y}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,x{y}^{x-1}⟩ \\ ∇g(1,e) & =⟨{e}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡e,1{e}^{1-1}⟩ \\  & =⟨e,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(1,e)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(1,e) & =∇g(1,e)\cdot u \\  & =⟨e,1⟩\cdot \frac{1}{5}⟨4,-3⟩ \\  & =\frac{e(4)+1(-3)}{5} \\  & =\frac{4e-3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

The rate of change of g(x,y) at the point (1,e) in the direction of v is equal to the directional derivative gu′(1,e).

First, we find the unit vector u in the direction of v: ‖v‖=42+(−3)2=5u=15⟨4,−3⟩

Now, we find the gradient ∇g(x,y) and evaluate it at the point (1,e): ∇g(x,y)=⟨∂∂x(yx),∂∂y(yx)⟩=⟨yxln⁡y,xyx−1⟩∇g(1,e)=⟨e1ln⁡e,1e1−1⟩=⟨e,1⟩

q-130811.name: Question 13
q-130811.problem: Consider the function $f(x,y)=2\sqrt{xy}.$ What is the rate of change of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(8,2)$ in the direction in which the function decreases most rapidly?
q-130811.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ decreases most rapidly in the opposite direction of its gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute $-∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(8,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}-∇f(x,y) & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\sqrt{xy})i-\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\sqrt{xy})j \\  & =-\sqrt{\frac{y}{x}}\,i-\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}\,j \\ -∇f(8,2) & =-\sqrt{\frac{2}{8}}\,i-\sqrt{\frac{8}{2}}\,j \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\,i-2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the rate of change of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(8,2)$ in the direction of $-∇f(8,2)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖-∇f(8,2)‖ & =‖-\frac{1}{2}\,i-2\,j‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}+4} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{17}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{17}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the function f(x,y)=2xy. What is the rate of change of f(x,y) at the point (8,2) in the direction in which the function decreases most rapidly?

b

c
43
d
46

104

Correct
EXPLANATION

At a given point, a function f(x,y) decreases most rapidly in the opposite direction of its gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute −∇f(x,y) and evaluate it at the point (8,2): −∇f(x,y)=−∂∂x(2xy)i−∂∂y(2xy)j=−yxi−xyj−∇f(8,2)=−28i−82j=−12i−2j

Finally, the rate of change of f(x,y) at the point (8,2) in the direction of −∇f(8,2) is given by ‖−∇f(8,2)‖=‖−12i−2j‖=(−12)2+(−2)2=14+4=174=172.

q-130806.name: Question 14
q-130806.problem: Consider the function $g(x,y)={x}^{y}.$ What is the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction in which the function increases most rapidly?
q-130806.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $g(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{y}),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{y})⟩ \\  & =⟨y{x}^{y-1},\,{x}^{y}\operatorname{ln}⁡x⟩ \\ ∇\,g(1,1) & =⟨(1){1}^{1-1},\,({1}^{1})\operatorname{ln}⁡1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of $∇g(1,1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖∇\,g(1,1)‖ & =‖⟨1,0⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

q-86543.name: Question 15
q-86543.problem: Consider the function $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x).$ What is the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{4},4)$ in the direction in which the function increases most rapidly?
q-86543.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $g(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(\frac{\pi }{4},4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x)),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x))⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{tan}⁡x,\,\frac{2}{y}⟩ \\ ∇\,g(\frac{\pi }{4},4) & =⟨-\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,\frac{2}{4}⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{4},4)$ in the direction of $∇g(\frac{\pi }{4},4)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖∇\,g(\frac{\pi }{4},4)‖ & =‖⟨-1,\frac{1}{2}⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{5}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

At a given point, a function g(x,y) increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

‖∇g(π4,4)‖=‖⟨−1,12⟩‖=1+14=54=52.
